name: NVIDIA Corporation
sum: The defining chipmaker of the AI era. NVIDIA's GPUs and CUDA software stack power the vast majority of large-scale AI training and inference, and its data-center segment dwarfs its legacy gaming business. Explosive earnings growth has made it one of the most valuable companies on earth. Its $500m OI cap — the largest of any single stock here — reflects how heavily traders lean on it. Bulls cite an entrenched software moat and insatiable compute demand; bears watch for custom-silicon competition, export controls, and any sign the AI capex cycle is cooling.

name: Tesla, Inc.
sum: An electric-vehicle maker the market prices as an AI and robotics company. Tesla leads Western EV production and energy storage, but its extreme valuation rests on future bets: full self-driving, the robotaxi network, and the Optimus humanoid robot. Earnings are modest relative to price, which is why its P/E sits in the hundreds. One of the most volatile large-caps in existence and a perennial favorite of leveraged traders — moves are amplified by Elon Musk's public profile, delivery numbers, and every incremental autonomy claim.

name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
sum: Google's parent and one of the cheapest mega-caps by P/E. Search and YouTube advertising fund everything, while Google Cloud has turned profitable and Gemini anchors its AI push. Waymo leads autonomous driving and DeepMind drives frontier research. The bear case is that AI chat could erode search dominance; the bull case is that Alphabet owns the models, the chips (TPUs), the cloud and the distribution. Ongoing antitrust cases are the main regulatory overhang.

name: Apple Inc.
sum: The world's most valuable consumer-hardware franchise. The iPhone remains the anchor, but Apple's growth story is now its high-margin Services business — the App Store, iCloud, payments and subscriptions layered on roughly two billion active devices. It has been slower on generative AI than peers, partnering out some capabilities. Enormous cash flows and relentless buybacks support the stock. Risks: iPhone upgrade fatigue, China exposure, regulatory pressure on App Store fees, and the perception it is playing catch-up in AI.

name: Microsoft Corporation
sum: A software giant reshaped into an AI-and-cloud powerhouse. Azure is the growth engine, Microsoft 365 and Windows are the cash base, and a deep partnership with OpenAI put Copilot across the entire product line. Enterprise lock-in is formidable and margins are elite. The debate centers on how quickly AI features convert into durable revenue versus the heavy capital spending on data centers required to serve them. Among the steadiest mega-caps, which is why it carries a high OI cap here.

name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
sum: Owner of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads — a digital-advertising machine reaching billions daily. AI-driven ad targeting and recommendation have reignited growth after a rough 2022. Meta open-sources its Llama models and spends aggressively on both AI infrastructure and its still-lossmaking Reality Labs metaverse division. The stock rewards ad strength and punishes any hint that the metaverse or AI capex is running ahead of returns. Regulatory and youth-safety scrutiny are constant.

name: Amazon.com, Inc.
sum: Two businesses in one: a global e-commerce and logistics empire, and AWS — the cloud unit that generates most of the profit. AWS growth, AI services and its Anthropic partnership are the swing factors for the stock, while retail margins improve with advertising and automation. Amazon reinvests almost everything, so reported earnings understate cash generation. Watch cloud growth rates, capex discipline, and antitrust attention on its marketplace and logistics dominance.

name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
sum: NVIDIA's chief challenger in AI accelerators and a share-gainer in server and PC CPUs. Its MI-series data-center GPUs are the credible number-two option for AI compute, and EPYC processors keep taking data-center share from Intel. The high P/E prices in rapid AI-driven growth, so any stumble in accelerator ramp or guidance hits hard. The bull thesis is a genuine two-horse race in AI silicon; the bear case is NVIDIA's software moat and AMD's execution risk.

name: Broadcom Inc.
sum: A semiconductor and infrastructure-software conglomerate that quietly became an AI heavyweight. Broadcom designs custom AI chips (ASICs) for hyperscalers and dominates high-speed networking silicon — the plumbing of AI data centers. Its VMware acquisition added a large, sticky enterprise-software base. Acquisitive, cash-generative and dividend-paying, it trades on custom-silicon demand from a handful of giant customers, which is also its concentration risk.

name: Micron Technology, Inc.
sum: One of the few makers of DRAM and NAND memory, and a direct beneficiary of the AI boom through high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used alongside AI GPUs. Memory is deeply cyclical, so Micron's earnings and P/E swing with supply-demand — cheap at the top of the cycle, expensive at the bottom. Its large $500m OI cap reflects heavy trader interest as an AI-adjacent, high-beta play. Watch HBM capacity, pricing, and the broader memory cycle.

name: Intel Corporation
sum: The former CPU king in the middle of a costly turnaround. Intel is pouring capital into its foundry ambitions to manufacture chips for others and reclaim process leadership from TSMC, while defending its data-center and PC franchises against AMD and Arm. Heavy spending and restructuring have compressed or erased profits, so a clean P/E is hard to pin down. A high-stakes bet: succeed at foundry and it re-rates; stumble and the cash burn bites. Politically important as a U.S. manufacturing champion.

name: Taiwan Semiconductor (TSMC)
sum: The world's most important company you rarely hear about. TSMC manufactures the advanced chips designed by NVIDIA, Apple, AMD and virtually everyone else — a near-monopoly on leading-edge fabrication. Its technology lead and pricing power are immense, and AI demand keeps its most advanced nodes sold out. The dominant risk is geopolitical: its concentration in Taiwan sits at the center of U.S.–China tension. Traded here as a U.S.-listed ADS.

name: SK hynix Inc.
sum: South Korea's memory champion and, crucially, the leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI accelerators — a position that made it one of the biggest single winners of the AI compute build-out. Like all memory makers it is cyclical, but HBM leadership has lifted margins and re-rated the story. Its large OI cap signals strong trader appetite. Priced in Korean won and converted to USD via oracle; low headline P/E is typical of the memory sector.

name: Samsung Electronics Co.
sum: A sprawling conglomerate spanning memory chips, smartphones (Galaxy), displays and consumer electronics, plus a contract chip-foundry unit chasing TSMC. Samsung is a memory heavyweight racing to catch SK hynix in HBM while defending its handset and display leadership. The diversified base makes it steadier than pure-play memory names but also slower-moving. Trades at a low P/E typical of Korean industrials; priced in won, oracle-converted to USD.

name: Marvell Technology, Inc.
sum: A data-infrastructure chipmaker riding AI networking and custom-silicon demand. Marvell builds the interconnects, optical DSPs and custom compute chips that move data inside AI data centers, and is a key partner for hyperscalers designing their own accelerators. Growth is tied to the same AI-capex wave as NVIDIA and Broadcom, giving it a healthy OI cap. Execution on custom-silicon wins and networking share drives the stock.

name: Qualcomm Incorporated
sum: The mobile-connectivity leader: Snapdragon processors and modem chips power much of the smartphone world, and its licensing business collects royalties across the industry. Qualcomm is diversifying into automotive, PCs and edge-AI to reduce handset dependence. A relatively low P/E reflects mature smartphone growth and concentration risk around key customers. On-device AI and its auto pipeline are the growth stories to watch.

name: Arm Holdings plc
sum: The architecture underneath nearly every smartphone and, increasingly, data-center and AI chips. Arm doesn't make chips — it licenses processor designs and collects royalties, a high-margin, asset-light model that commands a premium valuation. Its energy-efficient designs are spreading from mobile into servers, PCs and automotive as power efficiency becomes decisive for AI. British-headquartered, majority-owned by SoftBank, traded here as a U.S.-listed ADS.

name: ASML Holding N.V.
sum: A genuine monopoly at the heart of the chip world. ASML is the only company that makes extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines — the room-sized tools required to print the most advanced chips. Every leading-edge fab (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) depends on it. That makes ASML both indispensable and a geopolitical lever, since export controls limit which countries can buy its machines. Dutch-listed; traded here via a U.S. ADR.

name: Applied Materials, Inc.
sum: The largest supplier of semiconductor and display manufacturing equipment. Applied Materials sells the deposition, etching, implantation and inspection systems used to fabricate every chip, so it profits broadly from rising global chip capacity rather than any single design win. Growth tracks fab build-out and technology transitions; exposure to China export rules is a swing factor. A steadier, lower-P/E way to play the semiconductor cycle.

name: Western Digital Corporation
sum: A storage maker focused on hard-disk drives for the mass-capacity data-center market. As AI generates vast quantities of data that must be stored cheaply, demand for high-capacity drives has firmed. Storage is cyclical and lower-margin than compute, hence a modest P/E. Western Digital separated its flash-memory business (now Sandisk), leaving it a cleaner HDD play. Watch data-center capacity demand and drive pricing.

name: Sandisk Corporation
sum: The flash-memory and SSD business spun out of Western Digital, now trading as a standalone company. Sandisk makes NAND flash and solid-state storage for consumer devices, enterprise and data centers — a market lifted by AI's appetite for fast storage but subject to the same brutal memory cycles as DRAM. A large OI cap here suggests active trader interest in the newly independent name. Cyclical earnings keep the headline P/E low.

name: Kioxia Holdings Corporation
sum: Japan's flagship NAND-flash maker, formerly Toshiba Memory, and one of the handful of companies that control global flash supply. Kioxia's fortunes rise and fall with the memory cycle, and AI-driven storage demand has been a tailwind. Recently public on the Tokyo Stock Exchange; priced in yen and oracle-converted to USD. A cyclical, supply-driven story much like SK hynix and Micron on the NAND side.

name: Lumentum Holdings Inc.
sum: A photonics company making the lasers and optical components that move data at light speed inside AI data centers and telecom networks. The AI networking boom has revived demand for its high-speed optical transceivers and chips. Earnings have been recovering from a cyclical trough, so its trailing P/E is either very high or not meaningful. A more niche, higher-beta way to play AI interconnect demand alongside Marvell and Broadcom.

name: Cerebras Systems Inc.
sum: A challenger AI-chip company known for the wafer-scale engine — a single chip the size of a dinner plate built to train and run large models faster than clusters of conventional GPUs. Cerebras sells both systems and cloud AI compute, positioning itself as a NVIDIA alternative for certain workloads. Recently public and still scaling, so it has no meaningful P/E. A high-conviction, high-risk bet on differentiated AI hardware; sizeable OI cap for a young name.

name: Quantinuum Inc.
sum: A leading quantum-computing company built from Honeywell Quantum Solutions and Cambridge Quantum, developing trapped-ion quantum computers and quantum software. It's one of the most advanced players in a field that could eventually break current cryptography and transform chemistry and optimization — but commercial quantum advantage is still years out. Private and pre-IPO, so no public earnings or P/E. This market offers rare synthetic exposure to a name most investors can't otherwise access.

name: Oracle Corporation
sum: A database and enterprise-software veteran enjoying an unexpected second act as an AI-cloud provider. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure has won large contracts to host AI training workloads, and its backlog of signed cloud commitments has surged, re-rating a once-sleepy stock. The bull case is a genuine fourth hyperscaler emerging; the bear case is the enormous capex and debt required to build it, plus customer concentration. Watch cloud backlog conversion and margins.

name: ServiceNow, Inc.
sum: A workflow-automation platform that has become core plumbing for large enterprises' IT, HR and operations. ServiceNow is layering AI agents across its platform, a natural fit for automating repetitive corporate work. High retention, strong margins and reliable growth earn it a premium P/E. The debate is whether AI agents expand its market or eventually commoditize the workflows it sells. A steady large-cap software compounder.

name: International Business Machines
sum: The century-old tech institution reinvented around hybrid cloud (via Red Hat), consulting and enterprise AI (watsonx), with a side bet on quantum computing. IBM trades as a slower-growth, dividend-paying value name rather than a hyper-growth story. Its appeal is stability, cash flow and deep enterprise relationships; the risk is that growth stays modest while flashier rivals capture the AI narrative. A defensive way to hold big-tech exposure.

name: Palantir Technologies, Inc.
sum: A data-analytics and AI-software company serving governments and, increasingly, commercial enterprises. Its platforms integrate messy data for decision-making, and its AI Platform (AIP) has driven a wave of commercial growth. Palantir inspires unusually strong retail devotion and carries one of the highest P/E ratios in the market — priced for years of rapid growth. Any deceleration or valuation reset can be violent. A high-beta, high-narrative AI stock.

name: Zoom Communications, Inc.
sum: The video-meetings company that defined the pandemic era, now a profitable, cash-rich business hunting for growth beyond its core. Zoom is expanding into a broader collaboration suite — chat, phone, contact center and AI assistants — as meeting growth matured. A modest P/E reflects that transition. Notably, Zoom was an early strategic investor in Anthropic. The question is whether AI features and new products re-accelerate a stalled growth story.

name: Dell Technologies Inc.
sum: A PC and enterprise-infrastructure maker that turned into a surprise AI beneficiary. Dell's server business is booming as enterprises and cloud providers buy AI-optimized systems packed with GPUs, though those servers carry thinner margins than its traditional gear. The stock blends a steady PC/services base with an AI-server growth kicker. A reasonable P/E for a lower-margin hardware model; watch AI-server backlog and margin mix.

name: Netflix, Inc.
sum: The streaming leader that won the format it invented. After a growth scare, Netflix reignited results with a paid-sharing crackdown and a fast-growing ad tier, and it now generates substantial free cash flow. It's expanding into live events, gaming and advertising. The premium P/E prices continued subscriber and ad growth; risks include content costs, competition and saturation in mature markets. The clearest pure-play on streaming.

name: Coinbase Global, Inc.
sum: The largest publicly traded U.S. crypto exchange and a proxy for crypto adoption itself. Coinbase earns trading fees, custody and a growing stream of stablecoin and subscription revenue, and it operates the Base layer-2 network. Earnings are highly sensitive to crypto market cycles, so its P/E is volatile and cycle-dependent. Regulatory clarity in the U.S. is a major swing factor — friendlier rules expand its runway; crackdowns compress it.

name: Robinhood Markets, Inc.
sum: The app that mainstreamed commission-free trading for a younger generation, now a broadening fintech spanning stocks, options, crypto, retirement and cash management. Robinhood's revenue is tied to trading activity, crypto volumes and interest income, making it a high-beta play on retail engagement. It has pushed aggressively into crypto and tokenization itself. Profitable and growing, but its fortunes rise and fall with market enthusiasm and rates.

name: Circle Internet Group, Inc.
sum: The issuer of USDC, the second-largest dollar stablecoin, and one of the most important on-ramps between traditional dollars and crypto. Circle earns interest on the reserves backing USDC, so its revenue rises with both stablecoin supply and interest rates. A high-profile recent IPO, it trades on stablecoin adoption and regulatory tailwinds as the U.S. formalizes stablecoin rules. Earnings are rate-sensitive, and its valuation has been richly priced.

name: Strategy Inc. (MicroStrategy)
sum: Officially a software company, but in practice the largest corporate Bitcoin holder on the planet — a leveraged Bitcoin proxy dressed as an equity. Strategy raises debt and equity to buy and hold BTC, so its stock trades as an amplified bet on Bitcoin's price, often at a premium to the coins it owns. Accounting for its Bitcoin makes a conventional P/E meaningless. Extremely volatile; effectively a way to trade Bitcoin with equity-market plumbing.

name: Strategy 'Stretch' Preferred
sum: A variable-rate perpetual preferred share issued by Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) as part of its Bitcoin-treasury financing. Unlike the common stock, 'Stretch' pays cumulative cash dividends at a rate adjusted to keep its price near its $100 stated value — behaving more like a yield instrument than a growth stock. Being preferred equity, it has no P/E. This is a niche market for traders who want exposure to Strategy's capital structure rather than a direct Bitcoin bet.

name: Hyperliquid Strategies Inc.
sum: A digital-asset treasury company designed to give public-market investors exposure to HYPE, the native token of the Hyperliquid ecosystem — essentially a MicroStrategy-style vehicle, but for HYPE instead of Bitcoin. Its value tracks the tokens it holds, so a conventional P/E doesn't apply. A meta twist: it's a tokenized stock, trading on Hyperliquid, whose whole purpose is exposure to Hyperliquid's own token. High-beta and reflexive to HYPE's price.

name: Costco Wholesale Corporation
sum: The membership warehouse retailer with cult-like customer loyalty and remarkably consistent growth. Costco makes much of its profit from membership fees, letting it sell goods at razor-thin margins that keep members renewing at very high rates. That reliability earns it a premium P/E rare for a retailer. It's a defensive compounder — steady traffic, pricing discipline and dependable dividends. The debate is simply whether the valuation is too rich for its growth rate.

name: GameStop Corp.
sum: The video-game retailer turned meme-stock icon of 2021. GameStop's physical retail business is in secular decline, but it holds a large cash and (increasingly) crypto treasury, and its stock trades far more on retail-community sentiment than fundamentals. Earnings are minimal, so any P/E is distorted. Expect sharp, sentiment-driven moves detached from the underlying business — a favorite of leveraged, momentum-driven traders.

name: eBay Inc.
sum: The original online marketplace, now a mature, cash-generative business focused on used, refurbished and collectible goods rather than competing head-on with Amazon. eBay drives modest growth through 'focus categories,' advertising and payments, and returns cash via buybacks and dividends. A low P/E reflects slow growth and a value profile. Steady rather than exciting — a way to hold e-commerce exposure without a premium multiple.

name: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.
sum: China's e-commerce and cloud giant — Taobao, Tmall and Alibaba Cloud — and one of the country's leading AI developers via its Qwen models. Long weighed down by Chinese regulatory crackdowns and a weak consumer, the stock has swung on stimulus hopes and an AI-cloud re-rating. It offers cheap exposure to Chinese tech, but carries policy risk, U.S.-listing/delisting concerns and geopolitical overhang. Traded here as a U.S.-listed ADS.

name: Eli Lilly and Company
sum: The pharmaceutical company at the center of the obesity-drug boom. Lilly's GLP-1 therapies (tirzepatide) for diabetes and weight loss have become blockbusters, driving explosive revenue growth and one of the highest valuations in big pharma. It also has strong oncology, immunology and Alzheimer's pipelines. The premium P/E prices continued GLP-1 dominance; risks are manufacturing capacity, competition (notably Novo Nordisk), and pricing pressure. A rare high-growth story among healthcare mega-caps.

name: Hims & Hers Health, Inc.
sum: A direct-to-consumer digital-health platform offering telehealth consultations, prescriptions and wellness products for things like weight management, hair loss, sexual health and mental health. Hims rode the compounded-GLP-1 weight-loss wave and built a fast-growing subscription business with strong brand marketing. It's profitable and growing quickly, which supports a premium P/E. Risks include regulatory scrutiny of compounded drugs, competition, and reliance on marketing spend. A high-growth consumer-health name and a favorite of momentum traders.

name: Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX)
sum: Elon Musk's private space company and one of the most valuable startups in history — the market its largest OI cap here reflects intense demand for exposure. SpaceX dominates commercial launch via reusable rockets, operates Starlink's global satellite-internet network, and wholly owns the AI company xAI. Because it's private, there's no public P/E or share price; this synthetic market is one of the only ways to trade SpaceX at all. Valuation-driven and headline-sensitive.

name: Rocket Lab Corporation
sum: A publicly traded space company positioned as the credible number-two to SpaceX. Rocket Lab flies its small Electron rocket, is developing the larger reusable Neutron to compete for bigger payloads, and builds satellites and spacecraft components — an end-to-end space business. Still investing heavily and not yet consistently profitable, so no meaningful P/E. A high-growth, high-risk pure-play on the commercial space economy; very sensitive to launch cadence and Neutron progress.

name: Rivian Automotive, Inc.
sum: An American electric-vehicle maker focused on adventure trucks and SUVs, plus commercial delivery vans. Rivian has strong product reviews and a notable partnership and platform deal with Volkswagen, but it burns cash and isn't profitable, so it has no P/E. The stock hinges on ramping production, cutting costs and reaching its cheaper next-generation R2 model. A speculative EV growth play with real technology but real cash-runway risk.

name: Hyundai Motor Company
sum: One of the world's largest automakers, and a serious EV and hybrid competitor whose designs have won broad praise. Hyundai also owns a controlling stake in robotics firm Boston Dynamics, giving it an under-appreciated robotics angle. It trades at a strikingly low single-digit P/E, typical of the deep value placed on Korean industrials ('the Korea discount'). Priced in won, oracle-converted to USD. A cheap, cash-generative auto play with an embedded robotics option.

name: Bloom Energy Corporation
sum: A maker of solid-oxide fuel cells that generate on-site electricity for factories, hospitals and — increasingly — power-hungry AI data centers looking for fast, reliable capacity outside the strained grid. That data-center angle has driven renewed investor interest. Bloom hovers around breakeven, so its P/E is volatile or not meaningful. A leveraged bet on distributed power and the energy bottleneck behind the AI build-out; high-beta and news-driven.

name: USA Rare Earth, Inc.
sum: A company building a domestic U.S. supply chain for rare-earth elements and magnets — critical inputs for EVs, defense systems, robotics and electronics that China currently dominates. It's a policy-driven strategic story: Western governments want to onshore these materials. Still early-stage and largely pre-revenue, so no P/E. Extremely sensitive to rare-earth prices, government support and trade tensions with China. A speculative bet on supply-chain reshoring.

name: Blackstone Inc.
sum: The world's largest alternative-asset manager, overseeing enormous pools of private equity, real estate, credit and infrastructure capital. Blackstone earns management fees plus performance fees, so its earnings scale with assets and deal activity but can be lumpy. It's a bellwether for private markets and, increasingly, for financing the AI data-center build-out. Rate-sensitive: cheaper capital fuels dealmaking and real-estate values. A blue-chip way to hold private-markets exposure.

name: DraftKings Inc.
sum: A leading U.S. online sports-betting and iGaming operator riding the state-by-state legalization of sports wagering. DraftKings has been spending heavily on marketing to win market share, so profitability is only recently emerging and its P/E is high or not meaningful. Growth tracks new state launches, hold rates and user monetization. A high-beta consumer-tech play; sensitive to regulation, competition (FanDuel) and sports calendars.

name: BlackBerry Limited
sum: No longer a phone maker — today's BlackBerry is a software company centered on cybersecurity and its QNX embedded operating system, which runs in a huge share of the world's cars. The auto-software and IoT angle is the growth story; the cybersecurity unit is a turnaround. Earnings are thin, so the P/E is high or not meaningful. Canada-headquartered. A speculative software turnaround with a genuinely valuable embedded-systems franchise.

name: Nokia Corporation
sum: A Finnish telecom-infrastructure company — one of the few Western vendors of 5G network equipment alongside Ericsson, as operators seek alternatives to China's Huawei. Nokia sells to carriers and, increasingly, enterprises and data centers building private networks. It's a mature, dividend-paying value name with modest growth and a low P/E. Geopolitics (the shift away from Chinese vendors) is a structural tailwind; carrier capex cycles drive the swings.

name: CoreWeave, Inc.
sum: A specialized 'neocloud' that rents out GPU compute optimized for AI training and inference — effectively a picks-and-shovels landlord for the AI boom. CoreWeave grew explosively on huge contracts with AI labs and hyperscalers, but funds its GPU build-out with heavy debt and posts losses, so it has no P/E. The bull case is soaring AI-compute demand; the bear case is customer concentration, debt load and the risk of a GPU-capacity glut. Very high-beta.

name: Nebius Group N.V.
sum: An AI-cloud infrastructure company (the international business that emerged from the former Yandex, now Amsterdam-based) providing GPU clusters and full-stack tools for training and running AI models. Like CoreWeave, it's a fast-growing neocloud spending heavily to build capacity, so it's not yet profitable and has no meaningful P/E. A sizeable OI cap signals strong trader interest in AI-infrastructure exposure. Growth-and-capex driven; benefits directly from AI compute demand in Europe and beyond.

name: SharonAI Holdings Inc.
sum: An early-stage 'neocloud' providing GPU and high-performance computing infrastructure for AI workloads, building data-center capacity across Australia and the United States. It plays the same picks-and-shovels theme as CoreWeave and Nebius but is smaller and newer, making it more speculative. No meaningful P/E given its early stage. Exposure to the AI-compute build-out at the riskier, higher-upside end of the spectrum — highly sensitive to funding, contracts and execution.

name: NewBird AI (formerly Allbirds)
sum: An unusual story: the company once known for sustainable wool footwear (Allbirds) is pivoting toward becoming a GPU-as-a-service and AI-cloud provider. This kind of dramatic reinvention toward AI infrastructure makes the stock highly speculative and narrative-driven, with no meaningful P/E through the transition. Traders here are betting on the pivot's credibility rather than the legacy shoe business. Expect volatility tied to announcements about the AI strategy's substance.

name: RoboStrategy, Inc.
sum: A publicly listed closed-end investment company focused on robotics and 'embodied AI' — it holds equity and equity-linked stakes across private and public robotics, humanoid and physical-AI companies. Rather than one operating business, it's a basket bet on the robotics theme, so its value tracks its holdings and it has no conventional P/E. A way to gain diversified, thematic exposure to the humanoid-robot and physical-AI trend in a single ticker. Sentiment- and NAV-driven.

name: SoftBank Group Corp.
sum: A Japanese technology-investment holding company — effectively a giant, high-conviction AI portfolio. SoftBank owns a controlling stake in Arm, runs the Vision Fund, and has made huge bets across AI and semiconductors. Its stock trades on the value of those holdings (net asset value) and famously at a discount to them, so a P/E is only loosely meaningful. Volatile and reflexive to the AI trade and to Arm's share price. Priced in yen, oracle-converted to USD.

name: MiniMax Group
sum: A Chinese AI company building multimodal foundation models spanning text, audio, image, video, coding and agentic workflows — one of China's most prominent AI-application startups. Recently listed in Hong Kong, it's an early-stage, growth-and-investment story with no meaningful P/E yet. This market offers rare synthetic exposure to the Chinese frontier-AI race. Priced in Hong Kong dollars and oracle-converted to USD; carries the policy and geopolitical risk common to Chinese tech.

name: Zhipu AI / Z.ai
sum: One of China's leading large-model developers (also known as Z.ai), building general-purpose AI models and applications across coding, vision, audio, video and agents. A flagship of China's AI ecosystem, recently public in Hong Kong, still in heavy-investment mode with no meaningful P/E. Alongside MiniMax, it lets traders take a position on China's frontier-AI champions. Priced in Hong Kong dollars, oracle-converted to USD; exposed to Chinese tech policy and U.S.–China tech tensions.
